column4: The section's fallen columns and stakes gain a related image in Pharaoh's order to build a tower reaching toward heaven; this ayah makes his vertical construction an expression of the same worldly reach.
The next ayah completes the tower episode by exposing Pharaoh's plot as futile; it gives the section's human-built height a specific limit in Pharaoh's own context.

The section leaves angelic ranks standing after structures are flattened; this verse likens believers arranged in ranks to a compact building, a human formation that joins rank and structure in a contrasting way.
The oath by morning as it brightens gives another direct dawn formulation for the section's image of the first light standing out against darkness.
Clouds are driven, joined, and piled before rain and hail descend; this gives a volatile rain-cloud scene beside the section's cloud that appears to promise water but brings punishment.
The section reads moral فُجُور as tearing a religious cover; here accumulated wrongdoing leaves a rusting layer over hearts, an inverse covering image that marks the two outcomes of sin.

Those who do not expect to meet God are “رَضُوا بِالْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا وَاطْمَأَنُّوا بِهَا”; their contentment and settledness in this life directly reverse the section's soul returning contentedly to its Lord.
Their earned destination is the Fire; this neighboring consequence completes 10:7's contentment with worldly life and contrasts with the Garden awaiting the returning soul.

The verse joins a community identified as God's party, entry into Gardens, and mutual divine pleasure; it repeats the section's linked images of entering among servants and being pleased with one's Lord.

The earliest believers and those who follow them are gathered in the account of mutual pleasure and Gardens; this is a specific group-entry parallel to the section's soul admitted among God's servants.

When inheritance is being divided, needy relatives, orphans, and the poor who are present are to receive provision and kind words; this directly joins the section's inheritance shares, orphan, and table images.
The condemned person is described as one who did not urge feeding the poor, repeating the section's specific rebuke about withholding encouragement to feed the needy.
The next ayah says he has no close friend on that Day; this contributes the absence of human backing that the section joins to the solitary arrival.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's cause are warned of painful punishment; the verse directly links a person's stored wealth with what will not save him.
The hoarded metals are heated in Hell and used to brand their owners; this neighboring detail makes the consequence of 9:34's wealth-hoarding bodily and inescapable.
People who withhold God's bounty must not think it good for them; what they withheld becomes a collar on the Resurrection Day, reversing the section's claim that wealth proves honor.
Qarun is told to seek the Hereafter with what God has given him, do good, and not spread corruption; this directly corrects the section's image of wealth used for hoarding rather than care.
Qarun appears in his adornment, and people who desire worldly life wish they had what he received; this stages the section's mistaken reading of visible wealth as honor.

Those with knowledge answer that God's reward is better for the patient; this corrects the admiration of Qarun's wealth in 28:79 and echoes the section's distinction between possessions and genuine honor.
The owner of one of the two gardens boasts that he has greater wealth and more people; this closely stages the section's person who reads abundance as proof of being honored.

Entering his garden, the owner assumes it will never perish and doubts the Hour; this joins garden and wealth to a false belief in permanence, against the section's passing structures and lasting return.
The garden's water sinks into the earth so its owner cannot recover it; this is a precise reversal of the section's spring that servants can direct within the Garden.
The garden is ruined and its owner regrets what he spent on it; this brings the section's themes of wealth, earth, and belated regret into one scene.
No group can help the garden's owner against God; this is an exact social counterpart to the section's person arriving alone without anyone to support him.
After the garden owner loses it and has no helper, the passage declares that protection belongs to God, the True; this gives a fitting answer to the section's return to the Lord.
Righteousness includes giving wealth, despite love for it, to relatives, orphans, and the needy; this makes the section's wealth and orphan images meet in the opposite act of generosity.

After feeding the hungry and naming the orphan and destitute, the passage describes a community that urges patience and compassion; this connects the shared table to the section's soul joining God's servants.
Solomon asks to be admitted by God's mercy among His righteous servants; this is a close prayer-form parallel to the section's call for the soul to enter among the servants.
Joseph asks to die submitted and be joined with the righteous; this gives another specific formulation of the section's soul welcomed into a community at the end of its journey.
